sources.name: NOAA SWPC: estimated planetary K index, one-minute values
sources.use: The "Kp now" reading and the verdict for the present hour.

sources.name: NOAA SWPC: planetary K index, observed and 3-day forecast
sources.use: The Kp expected in each three-hour block of the next nights.

sources.name: NOAA SWPC: real-time solar wind, propagated to Earth
sources.use: Bz, speed, density and the time the solar wind takes to arrive.

sources.name: NOAA SWPC: OVATION aurora nowcast, hemispheric power
sources.use: The southern hemisphere power reading in gigawatts.

sources.name: NOAA SWPC: 27-day outlook of radio flux and geomagnetic indices
sources.use: The largest Kp expected each day for the next 27 days.

sources.name: NOAA SWPC: Tips on Viewing the Aurora
sources.use: The aurora's edge sits near 66 degrees magnetic latitude at Kp 0 and moves about 2 degrees per Kp step to 48 degrees at Kp 9. Best hours are around local midnight. A full moon dims what you see.

sources.name: NOAA SWPC: Tips on Viewing the Aurora (earlier version, still published)
sources.use: The aurora is easily seen when its edge is 4 to 5 degrees of magnetic latitude poleward of you.

sources.name: SpaceWeatherLive: The Kp-index
sources.use: The aurora's edge in magnetic latitude for each Kp value, from 64.5 degrees at Kp 1 to 48.1 degrees at Kp 9. These match NOAA's description of about 2 degrees per step.

sources.name: NOAA SWPC: Aurora 30-Minute Forecast
sources.use: Aurora does not need to be overhead: it can be seen from as much as 1000 km away when it is bright and conditions are right.

sources.name: NOAA Space Weather Scales
sources.use: Storm names G1 to G5, and how often each level occurs in an 11-year solar cycle: about 900 days at G1, 130 at G3 and 4 at G5.

sources.name: Bureau of Meteorology, Space Weather Services: geomagnetic indices and the northern limit of aurora visibility
sources.use: An independent check on the Kp each region needs: Kp 3 southern Tasmania, Kp 4 all of Tasmania, Kp 5 the Victorian coastline, Kp 6 the southwest coast of Western Australia, Kp 7 southern New South Wales, Kp 8 southern Queensland.

sources.name: Bureau of Meteorology, Space Weather Services: Aurora
sources.use: Australia's official Aurora Watch and Aurora Alert notices.

sources.name: Bureau of Meteorology: Catching the aurora (10 October 2018)
sources.use: Viewing advice: look south from a dark beach or hill, best around 10 pm to 2 am, most likely near the March and September equinoxes, and often grey to the eye at Australian latitudes.

sources.name: SpaceWeatherLive: OVATION auroral forecast
sources.use: How to read hemispheric power: under about 20 GW little or nothing to see, 20 to 50 GW you need to be near the aurora, over 50 GW plenty of activity.

sources.name: MET Norway: Locationforecast 2.0
sources.use: Hourly cloud cover for each place. Licensed under CC BY 4.0. The site shows the total cloud percentage unchanged apart from rounding.

sources.name: AACGM-v2 magnetic coordinates (Shepherd 2014, doi:10.1002/2014JA020264), via the aacgmv2 Python package
sources.use: Each place's magnetic latitude, computed for 17 November 2026 at ground level.

sources.name: SunCalc by Vladimir Agafonkin
sources.use: Darkness times, moon position and moon phase, calculated in your browser.

sources.name: International Meteor Organization: Meteor Shower Calendar 2026 (German edition)
sources.use: Geminids: activity 4 to 20 December, maximum 14 December 14h UT, ZHR 150, radiant at right ascension 112 and declination +33 degrees, population index 2.6, and the note that the southern hemisphere only gets the second half of the night.

sources.name: EarthSky: Geminid meteor shower
sources.use: A second peak prediction (14 December 05:44 UTC), the radiant's position near Castor, and the waxing crescent moon.

sources.name: Olech and others (2002), An artificial meteors database as a test for the presence of weak showers
sources.use: The zenithal hourly rate formula, used backwards to turn the ZHR into a count for a given radiant height and sky.

changelog.text: Added the Geminids 2026 page: radiant times, best-hour counts and a three-night cloud check for all 36 places.
First version: live go or no-go for 36 places in Australia and New Zealand, hour-by-hour view, next nights, 27-day outlook and a check for your own coordinates.
